title: Ezra 8:15–30
context: Ezra gathers the company at the river that runs to Ahava and, finding no Levites, sends leaders to Iddo at Casiphia to bring ministers for God’s house. Ezra 2:40 had already recorded only seventy-four Levites among the earlier returnees, so the shortage fits a pattern. By “the good hand of our God,” Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and others come, with 220 temple servants (8:18–20). Ezra proclaims a fast to seek a safe journey, because he was ashamed to ask the king for soldiers after declaring that God’s hand is on those who seek him; God grants the request (8:21–23). He then entrusts the silver, gold, and vessels to twelve leading priests, reminding them that they and the offering are holy to the LORD (8:24–30). Both traditions read the unit as shared ground on prayer, trust, and faithful stewardship; on how prayer relates to God’s purpose, the existing discussion at Joshua 10:14 applies, and no new contrast is added here.

verses.text: I gathered them together to the river that runs to Ahava; and there we encamped three days. Then I looked around at the people and the priests, and found there were none of the sons of Levi.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra gathers the company at the river to Ahava, camps three days, and finds no Levites among them. Arminian readers note Ezra’s careful review of the people. He recognizes a serious gap and takes responsibility for addressing it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Ezra’s attention to the needs of worship. Ezra 2:40 had recorded only seventy-four Levites in the first return, so the shortage fits a pattern. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing a leader who notices what God’s house will need and acts on it.

verses.text: Then I sent for Eliezer, for Ariel, for Shemaiah, for Elnathan, for Jarib, for Elnathan, for Nathan, for Zechariah, and for Meshullam, chief men; also for Joiarib and for Elnathan, who were teachers.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra sends for nine chief men and two teachers. Arminian readers note that Ezra involves others in solving the problem, choosing leaders and teachers for the mission. Wise leadership shares responsibility rather than acting alone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the care with which Ezra chooses his messengers, including men known for teaching. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a practical example of leadership and see no doctrinal question in the list of names.

verses.text: I sent them out to Iddo the chief at the place Casiphia; and I told them what they should tell Iddo and his brothers the temple servants at the place Casiphia, that they should bring to us ministers for the house of our God.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra sends them to Iddo, the chief at Casiphia, with instructions to ask for ministers for God’s house. Arminian readers note that Ezra tells them exactly what to say. Careful communication serves the goal of bringing Levites to the work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Ezra using appropriate channels to gather servants for God’s house. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as practical action taken in faith, with the outcome still to be seen in the following verses.

verses.text: According to the good hand of our God on us they brought us a man of discretion, of the sons of Mahli, the son of Levi, the son of Israel, namely Sherebiah, with his sons and his brothers, eighteen;
verses.arminianNotes: “According to the good hand of our God on us,” they bring Sherebiah, a man of discretion, with his sons and brothers. Arminian readers note that Ezra’s efforts succeed, and he credits God’s favor for the result. Human action and divine blessing meet.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s good hand as the decisive reason the Levites come. Shared ground: both traditions read the phrase as gracious providence and treat it as common ground; neither turns Ezra’s confession into a dispute about how God’s hand works alongside human action.

verses.text: and Hashabiah, and with him Jeshaiah of the sons of Merari, his brothers and their sons, twenty;
verses.arminianNotes: Hashabiah and Jeshaiah of the sons of Merari come with their relatives, twenty in all. Arminian readers note that more Levites respond to the call. Each one chose to join the journey and take up service in God’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God supplying the Levites who were lacking. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an answer to the need identified in 8:15, and both see in it God’s provision for the worship of his house.

verses.text: and of the temple servants, whom David and the princes had given for the service of the Levites, two hundred twenty temple servants. All of them were mentioned by name.
verses.arminianNotes: Two hundred twenty temple servants, all named, also come. Arminian readers note that these servants belonged to an order David and the princes had established. Their willingness to go supports the full range of service in the temple.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the continuity with David’s arrangements and the care taken to record each name. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as completing the provision of ministers for God’s house and affirm that every servant is known by name.

verses.text: Then I proclaimed a fast there at the river Ahava, that we might humble ourselves before our God, to seek from him a straight way for us, for our little ones, and for all our possessions.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra proclaims a fast at the river Ahava to humble themselves before God and seek a straight way for themselves, their children, and their possessions. Arminian readers see humble dependence on God expressed in prayer. Ezra seeks God’s protection rather than relying on his own resources.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the fast as a fitting expression of dependence on God. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a model of humble prayer before an uncertain journey; on how prayer relates to God’s purpose, the existing discussion at Joshua 10:14 applies, and no new contrast is added.

verses.text: For I was ashamed to ask of the king a band of soldiers and horsemen to help us against the enemy on the way, because we had spoken to the king, saying, “The hand of our God is on all those who seek him, for good; but his power and his wrath is against all those who forsake him.”
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra was ashamed to ask the king for soldiers, having said, “The hand of our God is on all those who seek him, for good.” Arminian readers note Ezra’s concern that his actions match his words. Seeking God and trusting him go together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Ezra’s concern for God’s honor before the king and his confidence in God’s protection. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an example of faith that refuses to undermine its own testimony, and both affirm that God’s hand is for good toward those who seek him.

verses.text: So we fasted and begged our God for this, and he granted our request.
verses.arminianNotes: “So we fasted and begged our God for this, and he granted our request.” Arminian readers see God answering the prayers of his people. The verse shows a real relationship in which God hears and responds to those who seek him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise affirm that God granted the request and see prayer as the means God used to bring about his good purpose. Shared ground: both traditions rejoice that God heard and answered, and the difference in how they relate prayer to God’s plan is already treated at Joshua 10:14.

verses.text: Then I set apart twelve of the chiefs of the priests, even Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten of their brothers with them,
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra sets apart twelve leading priests, including Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten of their brothers. Arminian readers note Ezra’s care in choosing trustworthy people to guard the offering. Responsibility is shared and clearly assigned.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see wise and orderly stewardship in Ezra’s arrangements. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an example of accountability in handling what belongs to God, and neither builds a doctrinal point on the number twelve.

verses.text: and weighed to them the silver, the gold, and the vessels, even the offering for the house of our God, which the king, his counselors, his princes, and all Israel there present, had offered.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra weighs out the silver, gold, and vessels offered by the king, his officials, and all Israel. Arminian readers note the transparency of the process. Weighing the gifts in front of witnesses guards against any suspicion of misuse.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see careful accountability for gifts dedicated to God. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a model of integrity in handling sacred resources, and both affirm that faithful stewardship honors God and protects his servants.

verses.text: I weighed into their hand six hundred fifty talents of silver, one hundred talents of silver vessels, one hundred talents of gold,
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra weighs out 650 talents of silver, 100 talents of silver vessels, and 100 talents of gold. Arminian readers note the enormous value entrusted to the priests. The size of the offering makes the need for faithfulness and protection all the greater.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the great wealth and the trust placed in those who carry it. Shared ground: both traditions read the figures as part of the historical account, decline to build doctrine on the amounts, and see in them the generosity directed to God’s house.

verses.text: twenty bowls of gold weighing one thousand darics, and two vessels of fine bright bronze, precious as gold.
verses.arminianNotes: Twenty gold bowls worth a thousand darics and two vessels of fine bronze, precious as gold, complete the inventory. Arminian readers note the careful recording of each item. Nothing is left vague, which protects both the offering and those who carry it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see thoroughness in the inventory and the value placed on even the bronze vessels. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of a careful record of stewardship, with no doctrinal question raised by the items.

verses.text: I said to them, “You are holy to the LORD, and the vessels are holy. The silver and the gold are a free will offering to the LORD, the God of your fathers.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra tells the priests, “You are holy to the LORD, and the vessels are holy,” and the offering is freewill, given to the God of their fathers. Arminian readers note the call to holiness that accompanies the task. Those set apart for God must act accordingly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the priests and vessels set apart for God and the offering as a willing gift. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as linking holiness of person and of purpose, and both affirm that service to God calls for a life consecrated to him.

verses.text: Watch and keep them until you weigh them before the chiefs of the priests, the Levites, and the princes of the fathers’ households of Israel at Jerusalem, in the rooms of the LORD’s house.”
verses.arminianNotes: The priests are to guard the offering until it is weighed again in Jerusalem before the leaders, in the rooms of the LORD’s house. Arminian readers note the accountability built into the journey. They must deliver exactly what they received.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a careful system of checks that honors God and protects his servants. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a model of faithful stewardship, in which those entrusted with God’s gifts are accountable for them.

verses.text: So the priests and the Levites received the weight of the silver, the gold, and the vessels, to bring them to Jerusalem to the house of our God.
verses.arminianNotes: The priests and Levites receive the silver, gold, and vessels to bring them to Jerusalem. Arminian readers note their acceptance of a weighty responsibility. They take up the task willingly, trusting God for the journey ahead.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see faithful servants receiving a sacred trust. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as completing the preparations for the journey, with the offering entrusted to those set apart for God’s service.
